content: In many cultures, a grain is a unit of mass approximately equivalent to the weight of a single seed from a typical cereal crop. For example, in Europe, the average mass of wheat or barley grains was historically used to define mass units, such as 79.891 milligrams. The grain is the only unit shared by all three traditional English mass and weight systems: avoirdupois, apothecaries’, and troy systems. Specifically, one grain is equivalent to 0.077 grams. Grains are utilized in various fields. In fencing, grains are used to measure the weight of tools, including the foil. In archery, grains are employed to measure the weight of arrows and their components. Additionally, grains are used in environmental permitting to quantify particulate emissions. They are also used to measure the amount of moisture per cubic foot of air, which is a measure of absolute humidity. Historically, grains of wheat or barley were used in the Mediterranean region to define units of mass, along with other seeds, particularly those of the carob tree. According to a longstanding tradition, one carat (the mass of a carob seed) was equivalent to the weight of four wheat grains or three barleycorns. However, the weights of these seeds are highly variable, especially for cereals, as they depend on moisture content. Thus, this equivalence is more of a convention than an absolute standard. During the reign of Henry III of England, the traditional interpretation of historical texts suggests that they referred to the troy pound, with references to sterling pennies being symbolic. The Tower pound, abolished in 1527, consisted of 12 ounces like the troy pound but was 1/16 lighter. To make sense of the historical texts, one must substitute 24 barley grains for the 32 wheat grains mentioned, following the general 4:3 equivalence convention. The original sterling pennies weighed 22.5 troy grains or 24 Tower grains if the Tower pound was divided similarly to the troy pound. Regardless of which pound the text originally referred to, a troy ounce equals 480 troy grains (20 × 24), and a troy pound consists of 5,760 grains (12 × 20 × 24). Initially, the troy pound was used for weighing items like pence, spices, and confections, while merchants used different standards compatible with international trade. One such standard, the avoirdupois pound, was later officially fixed at exactly 7,000 troy grains. It consists of 16 avoirdupois ounces, each weighing 437.5 troy grains.
